slides.headline: The 'killer whale' is the world's biggest dolphin.
slides.sub: Its name gets the family wrong. Here is what it really is

slides.headline: Whale by name, dolphin by family
slides.body: Orcas belong to Delphinidae, the oceanic dolphin family. Dolphins are toothed whales, and the orca is the largest member of that family.

slides.label: length of the largest males, at about 9,800 kg
slides.body: An older male's straight dorsal fin can stand 1.8 m tall. Females reach about 8.5 m, with a fin about half that height.

slides.headline: Mum's group, for life
slides.body: In fish-eating 'resident' populations of the northeastern Pacific, offspring do not disperse: sons and daughters stay in their mother's group (matriline).

slides.headline: Every pod has its own dialect
slides.body: Each Pacific Northwest pod has a unique set of calls. The calls are learned and culturally passed between individuals, not inherited.

slides.headline: One species, many menus
slides.body: Residents eat mainly salmon, transients hunt marine mammals and squid, offshore orcas take fish including sharks. Some Antarctic orcas hunt seals.

slides.headline: Send this to someone who loves orcas.
slides.body: IUCN lists the orca as Data Deficient (2017). Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
The killer whale or orca (Orcinus orca) is the largest member of the dolphin family, despite its name.

The name likely comes from sailors who watched orcas hunt large marine animals and called them 'whale killers', which later flipped to 'killer whale'. Wild orcas are found in every ocean, from the polar ice to the equator.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: NOAA Fisheries; Britannica; Williams & Lusseau (2006), Biology Letters; IUCN Red List (2017).
